title: OOP in practice
scopeHtml: Scope: composition over inheritance, dependency injection in practice, decorator/strategy/adapter/facade, testing with mocks and fakes, code smells and refactorings.

notes.title: Composition over inheritance
notes.html:
Inheritance says "is-a"; composition says "has-a". Prefer composition: build a class by holding other objects and forwarding to them. It stays flexible because you can swap parts at runtime, while inheritance fixes the relationship at compile time and exposes the parent's internals (fragile base class).

// Inheritance trap: counting adds via HashSet subclass
class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    int count;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { count++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { count += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); } // addAll calls add -> double count!
}

// Composition: wrap and forward
class CountingSet2<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner = new HashSet<>(); private int count;
    boolean add(E e) { count++; return inner.add(e); }
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { boolean ch = false; for (E e : c) ch |= add(e); return ch; }
}
// Kotlin delegation = composition with no boilerplate
class Logging(private val inner: Repo) : Repo by inner {
    override fun save(x: Item) { println("saving $x"); inner.save(x) }
}

Worked example. CountingSet with addAll(3 items) reports 6 not 3 because HashSet.addAll internally calls add. The bug exists only because the subclass depends on the parent's internal call pattern, which can change in the next JDK.

When inheritance is right. A real is-a with a stable base you control, the parent is designed for extension (documented hooks), and Liskov holds.

Industry examples. Android favours composition: Fragment plus ViewModel, Compose functions instead of View subclasses. Go has no inheritance at all. Effective Java Item 18: "Favor composition over inheritance".

Decision gravity. Composition is easy to change later (swap the part). Deep inheritance trees are a one-way door once clients subclass.

Everyday analogy. A car has an engine; it is not a kind of engine. You can change engines without changing the idea of a car.

Common interview traps.

  • Inheriting just to reuse code (use delegation).
  • Saying "never use inheritance"; design for it or forbid it (final).
  • Not knowing the fragile base class problem.

notes.title: Dependency injection in practice
notes.html:
DI means passing collaborators in rather than creating them inside. In practice: constructor parameters, one composition root, and optionally a framework.

Choices:

  • Manual DI: plain constructors in main/Application. Zero magic, fine up to about 50 classes.
  • Runtime container (Spring): reflection, quick to write, errors appear at startup.
  • Compile-time (Dagger/Hilt): code generated, errors at build, no reflection (important on Android startup time).
  • Koin (service-locator style DSL): simple, but errors at runtime.
class App {
    public static void main(String[] a) {                    // composition root
        var repo = new JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource());
        var pay = new StripeGateway(System.getenv("KEY"));
        var svc = new OrderService(repo, pay, Clock.systemUTC());
        new HttpServer(svc).start();
    }
}
@HiltViewModel
class OrderViewModel @Inject constructor(private val repo: OrderRepository, private val clock: Clock) : ViewModel()

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class DataModule { @Binds abstract fun repo(impl: RoomOrderRepository): OrderRepository }

Scopes. Singleton (one per app), per-request/per-screen (one per ViewModel), unscoped (new each time). Leaking an Activity into a singleton is the classic Android memory leak.

Worked example. Inject Clock instead of calling Instant.now(): a test pins time to 2026-01-01 and asserts a coupon expires. Without it the test depends on the real date and fails randomly.

Industry examples. Spring Boot (reflection DI, startup 2 to 10 s for big apps), Google Guice, Dagger at Google/Square, Hilt on Android.

Decision gravity. Choosing a DI framework is moderately sticky (annotations spread through code). Plain constructors keep you framework-free and reversible.

Everyday analogy. An electrician fits appliances into your wiring plan once; you do not run wires in each room yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Field injection (@Autowired on a field) hides dependencies and hampers tests.
  • Circular dependencies between services; a design smell, not a container bug.
  • Injecting the container itself (service locator).

notes.title: Composition patterns: decorator, strategy, adapter, facade
notes.html:
Four small patterns do most of the real work.

Decorator  wraps same interface, adds behaviour   (logging, caching, retry)
Strategy   swaps an algorithm behind an interface (pricing, sorting)
Adapter    converts one interface into another    (legacy SDK -> your port)
Facade     one simple front for a messy subsystem (checkout() hides 6 services)
interface Fetcher { String get(String url); }
class HttpFetcher implements Fetcher { public String get(String u){ /* network */ return "body"; } }
class CachingFetcher implements Fetcher {                 // decorator
    private final Fetcher next; private final Map<String,String> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    CachingFetcher(Fetcher next) { this.next = next; }
    public String get(String u) { return cache.computeIfAbsent(u, next::get); }
}
Fetcher f = new CachingFetcher(new HttpFetcher());       // stack decorators like Lego
class RetryFetcher(private val next: Fetcher, private val tries: Int = 3) : Fetcher {
    override fun get(url: String): String {
        repeat(tries - 1) { try { return next.get(url) } catch (e: java.io.IOException) { Thread.sleep(200L shl it) } }
        return next.get(url)
    }
}

Worked example. Cache TTL 60 s with a 90% hit rate on an API of 100 ms: average latency drops to about 0.1 x 100 + 0.9 x 1 = 11 ms, a 9x gain, and the HTTP class was not touched (OCP).

Industry examples. OkHttp interceptors are decorators; Java BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(...)); Retrofit Converter.Factory (adapter); Spring @Cacheable and @Retryable apply decorators with proxies; Android Repository as a facade over Room and Retrofit.

Everyday analogy. Wrapping a gift: each layer adds something, and the gift inside is unchanged.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up decorator (same interface, extra behaviour) and adapter (different interface).
  • Wrapper order matters: retry outside cache vs inside gives different results.
  • Facade turning into a God class.

notes.title: Testing with mocks, fakes and stubs
notes.html:
Test doubles stand in for real collaborators. Stub: returns canned answers. Fake: a lightweight working version (in-memory repo). Mock: records and verifies interactions. Spy: wraps the real object.

Use the cheapest double that works: fakes for state, stubs for inputs, mocks only for outgoing side effects that matter (emails sent, payment charged once).

@Test void chargesOnce() {
    var gateway = mock(PaymentGateway.class);
    when(gateway.charge(any(), eq(500))).thenReturn(Receipt.ok());
    var svc = new OrderService(new InMemoryRepo(), gateway);
    svc.place(cartOf(500));
    verify(gateway, times(1)).charge(any(), eq(500));
}
@Test fun chargesOnce() = runTest {
    val gateway = mockk<PaymentGateway>()
    every { gateway.charge(any(), 500) } returns Receipt.ok()
    OrderService(FakeRepo(), gateway).place(cartOf(500))
    verify(exactly = 1) { gateway.charge(any(), 500) }
}

Test pyramid. About 70% unit tests (ms each), 20% integration (real DB via Testcontainers, seconds), 10% end to end (minutes). Unit tests on pure logic need no mocks at all.

Worked example. Over-mocking: a test with 8 mocks and verify on every internal call breaks on each refactor even though behaviour is unchanged (brittle). Replace mocks with a fake repo and assert on the outcome (repo.find(id).status == PAID), and the test survives refactoring.

Industry examples. Mockito and MockK; Android Room in-memory DB for fast tests; Testcontainers (Postgres in Docker) at Netflix-scale teams; contract tests (Pact) between services.

Decision gravity. Mock only types you own; wrap third-party SDKs behind your interface and mock that. Mocking a library directly couples tests to its internals.

Everyday analogy. A crash-test dummy and a flight simulator: they let you test without real danger.

Common interview traps.

  • Verifying implementation details (call order, private calls).
  • Mocking value objects or the class under test.
  • Tests that need the real clock, network or random numbers; inject them.

notes.title: Common code smells
notes.html:
A code smell is a surface hint that the design may be wrong. Not a bug, but a reason to look.

Smell                       What it looks like                         Likely cure
-------------------------   ----------------------------------------   -------------------------
Long method                 > 30 lines, many comment headings          Extract method
God class                   2,000 lines, many unrelated fields         Extract class (SRP)
Long parameter list         7+ params                                  Parameter object / builder
Feature envy                method uses another class's data most     Move method
Shotgun surgery             one change, edits in 8 files               Move/inline, group by change
Divergent change            one class edited for many reasons          Split (SRP)
Primitive obsession         String phone, double money                 Value object (Money, Phone)
Switch on type              growing when/if by type                    Polymorphism / strategy
Duplicate code              copy-paste blocks                          Extract method/class
Data clump                  same 3 fields travel together             Make a class
Speculative generality      interface with one impl, never extended    Delete it (YAGNI)
Message chain               a.b().c().d()                              Hide delegate (Demeter)
Mutable global state        static mutable singleton                   Inject, make immutable

Worked example. double price everywhere: a rounding bug (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004) in invoices. Fix: Money(long cents, Currency); arithmetic is exact integer maths and the compiler stops you adding rupees to dollars.

Industry examples. Static analysers (SonarQube, Detekt, Android Lint, ktlint) flag several automatically (cyclomatic complexity above 10, method length). Fowler's "Refactoring" catalogue is the standard vocabulary.

Everyday analogy. A smell in the kitchen is a clue to check the fridge before anyone gets sick.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming smells without cures.
  • Treating all duplication as bad (two things that merely look alike may change independently).
  • Calling every long method a smell without checking readability.

notes.title: Refactoring step by step
notes.html:
Refactoring changes structure without changing behaviour. The safe loop: (1) get a test around the code (a characterization test records current output), (2) make one small change, (3) run tests, (4) commit. Never refactor and add features in the same commit.

Common moves: Extract Method, Rename, Move Method, Extract Class, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Introduce Parameter Object, Replace Primitive with Value Object, Inline.

// BEFORE
double total(Order o) {
    double t = 0;
    for (Item i : o.items) t += i.price * i.qty;
    if (o.customer.equals("VIP")) t *= 0.9;
    if (t > 1000) t -= 50;
    return t;
}

// AFTER (extract + replace conditional with strategy)
double total(Order o) {
    Money subtotal = o.subtotal();
    return discounts.stream().reduce(subtotal, (m, d) -> d.apply(o, m), (a, b) -> b).value();
}
fun total(o: Order): Money = discounts.fold(o.subtotal()) { m, d -> d.apply(o, m) }

Worked example. A 400-line checkout method refactored over 6 commits of about 20 minutes each; at every commit the 40 tests stay green. A single big rewrite would leave 3 days with nothing deployable.

Industry examples. IDE refactorings (IntelliJ and Android Studio rename, extract, move are automated and safe); Google's large-scale changes (Rosie) are mechanical refactorings; the Strangler Fig pattern replaces legacy modules piece by piece.

Decision gravity. Refactor when you are about to change the code ("boy scout rule"), not on a whim. Small steps are fully reversible; big-bang rewrites rarely are.

Everyday analogy. Reorganising a shop while it stays open: one shelf at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Refactoring without tests.
  • Mixing behaviour change with structure change.
  • Rewriting from scratch (second-system effect).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Prefer composition and delegation; inheritance only for a true, stable is-a you control; beware fragile base class.
  • DI: constructor injection, one composition root; manual DI is fine for small apps; Hilt/Dagger compile-time, Spring runtime; avoid field injection and service locator.
  • Decorator (same interface plus behaviour), strategy (swap algorithm), adapter (convert interface), facade (simplify subsystem).
  • Tests: fakes for state, stubs for inputs, mocks for side effects; inject clock/network; mock only what you own; avoid brittle verifications.
  • Smells: long method, God class, primitive obsession, switch on type, feature envy, shotgun surgery; each has a named cure.
  • Refactor in small, test-covered steps; never mix refactoring with new features.

questions.promptHtml: Why do people say "favour composition over inheritance"? When is inheritance still right?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates dogma from judgement; it is the base of most design discussions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Inheritance couples a subclass to the parent's internals (fragile base class) and is fixed at compile time. Composition holds a collaborator and forwards, so I can swap parts and keep encapsulation. Inheritance is right for a real, stable is-a with a base designed for extension, where Liskov holds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Inheritance reuses code AND exposes implementation: a subclass depends on which parent methods call which. Composition reuses code through a narrow interface. Kotlin's by delegation removes the forwarding boilerplate.

is-a  : Dog extends Animal       (shared contract, stable)
has-a : Car has Engine           (swap parts, test with fakes)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Logging implements Repo {
    private final Repo inner;
    Logging(Repo inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public void save(Item x) { System.out.println("saving " + x); inner.save(x); }
}
class Logging(private val inner: Repo) : Repo by inner {
    override fun save(x: Item) { println("saving $x"); inner.save(x) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Inheriting purely to reuse code.
  • Saying "never inherit"; design for extension or mark final.
  • Deep hierarchies where one change ripples to all subclasses.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the fragile base class problem? -> A parent change silently breaks subclasses relying on internals.
  2. What is Liskov substitution? -> Subtypes must be usable wherever the base is expected without surprising callers.
  3. How do you migrate a hierarchy away from inheritance? -> Extract an interface, introduce a delegate, move behaviour, then remove the extends.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average repeats the slogan. Senior gives criteria (stable is-a, extension hooks, LSP) and a migration path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A subclass of a framework base class broke on a minor upgrade when the base changed its internal call order.

questions.promptHtml: What is dependency injection and why does it matter beyond using Spring or Hilt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates equate DI with a framework; the principle is plain constructors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DI means a class receives its collaborators instead of creating them. It makes dependencies explicit and swappable, so I can test with fakes and change implementations without editing the class. A framework is optional; a composition root with plain constructors is DI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Prefer constructor injection: final fields, impossible to build half-initialized, and the constructor signature shows the dependencies. One composition root (main/Application) wires the graph. Options: manual (fine to about 50 classes), runtime container (Spring: reflection, errors at startup), compile-time (Dagger/Hilt: generated code, errors at build), Koin (runtime DSL).

main -> JdbcRepo -> OrderService <- StripeGateway

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var repo = new JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource());
var svc  = new OrderService(repo, new StripeGateway(key), Clock.systemUTC());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Field injection hiding dependencies.
  • Injecting the container (service locator).
  • Circular dependencies treated as a container bug.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why inject Clock? -> Deterministic tests for time logic.
  2. Hilt vs Spring? -> Compile-time versus reflection, startup time on Android.
  3. What scopes exist? -> Singleton, per-request or per-screen, unscoped.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average names a framework. Senior argues for constructor injection, a single root, and scope discipline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hidden new HttpClient() inside a service made a test hit production once.

questions.promptHtml: Distinguish decorator, strategy, adapter and facade with one real example each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks for vocabulary and for the common confusion between decorator and adapter.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Decorator wraps the same interface to add behaviour (caching, retry). Strategy swaps an algorithm behind an interface (pricing). Adapter converts one interface to another (legacy SDK to my port). Facade is one simple entry point over a messy subsystem (checkout()).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decorator  same interface in/out, adds behaviour   OkHttp interceptors, BufferedInputStream
Strategy   interchangeable algorithm               Comparator, pricing rules
Adapter    different interface -> expected one     Retrofit converters
Facade     simplified API over many parts          Android Repository over Room+Retrofit

Order matters: Retry(Cache(Http)) vs Cache(Retry(Http)) behave differently.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Fetcher f = new RetryFetcher(new CachingFetcher(new HttpFetcher()), 3);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling an adapter a decorator.
  • Facade growing into a God class.
  • Strategy for a single implementation (speculative generality).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does Spring use decorators? -> Proxies for @Cacheable, @Transactional, @Retryable.
  2. Strategy vs state? -> State changes itself; strategy is chosen from outside.
  3. Cache TTL 60 s, 90% hits on 100 ms API? -> Average about 11 ms.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average defines each. Senior discusses ordering, open/closed benefits, and misuse.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Retry placed outside the cache replayed cached failures for a minute.

questions.contextHtml:
A metrics wrapper counts how many elements were added to a set. After a JDK upgrade the dashboard shows exactly double the expected count for bulk adds.

class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    int count;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { count++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        count += c.size(); return super.addAll(c);
    }
}
var s = new CountingSet<String>();
s.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
System.out.println(s.count);   // 6

Red herring: "the JDK introduced a bug".
questions.promptHtml: Why 6, and how do you restructure it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the count += in addAll." Works today, breaks if the parent's implementation changes again.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must it be a Set for callers? Thread safety? Which methods mutate (remove, clear)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete the double count in addAll and pin the behaviour with a test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) AbstractCollection.addAll calls add per element, so each is counted twice; (b) the JDK changed (documented implementation detail); (c) another override.
  4. How I'd verify each: Print a stack trace in add; read the JDK source; test addAll of 3 items.
  5. Root cause: Self-use of overridable methods in the parent leaks into the subclass contract.
  6. Fix: composition.
class CountingSet<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner = new HashSet<>(); private int count;
    boolean add(E e) { count++; return inner.add(e); }
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { boolean ch = false; for (E e : c) ch |= add(e); return ch; }
}

To remain a Set, extend ForwardingSet (Guava) or use Kotlin Set<E> by inner. 7. Prevention: Review rule "do not subclass concrete collections"; design for extension or mark final. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not rely on documented-by-observation behaviour; composition costs a bit of forwarding code.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicate adds counted? -> Count only when inner.add returns true.
  • Thread safety? -> Wrap with a lock or AtomicLong.
  • Kotlin? -> class CountingSet<E>(private val s: MutableSet<E>) : MutableSet<E> by s.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An audit subclass of a collection undercounted after a library tuned addAll; the wrapper rewrite ended the dependence on internals.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes a line without understanding.
  • Hire: explains self-use and composes.
  • Strong hire: gives forwarding option and test strategy.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between stub, fake, mock and spy, and how do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-mocked suites are a classic maintainability problem; interviewers want judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A stub returns canned answers, a fake is a lightweight working implementation (in-memory repo), a mock records and verifies interactions, a spy wraps the real object. I use the cheapest that works: fakes for state, stubs for inputs, mocks only for outgoing side effects that matter, like "payment charged once".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Verifying internal calls ties the test to the implementation; asserting on outcomes survives refactoring. Mock only types you own: wrap third-party SDKs behind your interface and mock that. Pyramid: about 70% unit, 20% integration (Testcontainers), 10% end-to-end. Inject clock, network and randomness.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test fun chargesOnce() = runTest {
    val gateway = mockk<PaymentGateway>()
    every { gateway.charge(any(), 500) } returns Receipt.ok()
    OrderService(FakeRepo(), gateway).place(cartOf(500))
    verify(exactly = 1) { gateway.charge(any(), 500) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mocking the class under test or value objects.
  • Verifying call order of private details.
  • Mocking third-party types directly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a fake better than a mock? -> When behaviour over state matters.
  2. Risk of fakes? -> They can drift; run contract tests against both fake and real.
  3. Spies? -> Useful for legacy code, but a smell for new code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average knows the names. Senior ties choice to refactor resilience and contract tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A suite with 8 mocks per test broke on every refactor, so engineers stopped trusting it.

questions.contextHtml:
A Spring service fails to start after a PR adds a notification feature. Staging boot time is also now 14 s (was 6 s). The test for OrderService needs a full Spring context (11 s) because dependencies are field-injected.

@Service class OrderService {
    @Autowired private NotificationService notifier;
    @Autowired private InventoryService inventory;
}
@Service class NotificationService { @Autowired private OrderService orders; }
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:
   orderService -> notificationService -> orderService

Red herring: "set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Enables circular references or uses @Lazy; the design problem remains.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why does notification need orders? Which direction is the real dependency? Is the call synchronous?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Temporarily break the cycle with an event publication instead of a direct call.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) responsibilities wrongly split; (b) notification only needs order data, not the service; (c) a shared helper is missing.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dependency graph (jdeps/IDE diagram), method usage grep.
  5. Root cause: A bidirectional dependency between two services is a design smell; field injection hid it.
  6. Fix: constructor injection, pass the data, publish an event.
@Service class OrderService {
    private final InventoryService inventory; private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    OrderService(InventoryService i, ApplicationEventPublisher e) { inventory = i; events = e; }
    void place(Order o) { /* ... */ events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(o.id())); }
}

The notifier listens to OrderPlaced; unit test builds new OrderService(fakeInventory, publisher) in milliseconds. 7. Prevention: Constructor injection only; ArchUnit rules against cycles; disable circular references. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Events add indirection and eventual consistency; I would not use @Lazy as a permanent fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is constructor injection better for the cycle? -> It fails immediately and makes the cycle impossible to hide.
  • Would a third class help? -> Yes, extract the shared logic.
  • Hilt equivalent? -> Dagger reports cycles at compile time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" @Lazy hid a cycle for two years until a refactor caused a stack overflow at startup.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: toggles the property.
  • Hire: breaks the cycle with redesign and constructor injection.
  • Strong hire: ArchUnit, event trade-offs, faster tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A coupon test passes locally and fails randomly in CI at midnight UTC and on the 1st of each month.

class CouponService {
    boolean isValid(Coupon c) { return Instant.now().isBefore(c.expiresAt()); }
    String newCode() { return "C" + new Random().nextInt(1_000_000); }
}
@Test void validToday() {
    var c = new Coupon(Instant.now().plus(1, ChronoUnit.SECONDS));
    assertTrue(new CouponService().isValid(c));      // flaky on slow CI
}

Red herring: "the CI machine's clock is skewed".
questions.promptHtml: Why is it flaky and how do you restructure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds Thread.sleep or increases the 1 second margin.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Other uses of now() and random? Do we need real time in production only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Widen the margin to stop the red CI while refactoring.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) test depends on wall clock; (b) 1 s margin is eaten by GC/CI latency; (c) timezone/date boundary logic elsewhere.
  4. How I'd verify each: run the test 1,000 times under CPU load; search for now().
  5. Root cause: Hidden dependency on the system clock (and RNG) makes behaviour non-deterministic.
  6. Fix: inject Clock and an id generator.
class CouponService {
    private final Clock clock; private final IntSupplier ids;
    CouponService(Clock clock, IntSupplier ids) { this.clock = clock; this.ids = ids; }
    boolean isValid(Coupon c) { return clock.instant().isBefore(c.expiresAt()); }
}
// test: Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC)
  1. Prevention: Ban Instant.now()/new Random() outside the composition root (ArchUnit or lint).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not mock static now() with PowerMock; it hides the dependency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Coroutines? -> Use TestScope virtual time.
  • Time zones? -> Use Clock with a zone; test across DST.
  • Scheduled jobs? -> Inject a scheduler.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A subscription renewal bug appeared only on month-end; with an injected clock the team reproduced it in one test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sleeps or retries the test.
  • Hire: injects Clock.
  • Strong hire: adds RNG, lint rule, DST/boundary tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A product-catalog client is wired as a decorator stack. During a 90-second upstream outage, users keep seeing errors for 60 more seconds after the upstream recovers, and upstream sees 3x normal traffic during the outage.

Fetcher f = new CachingFetcher(new RetryFetcher(new HttpFetcher(), 3));
// Caching(Retry(Http)): cache stores whatever Retry returns
class RetryFetcher { /* returns "" on exhaustion instead of throwing */ }
12:01:03 GET /p/42  upstream 503 x3 -> RetryFetcher returns ""  -> cached (TTL 60s)
12:02:40 upstream healthy; GET /p/42 -> cache hit -> ""

Red herrings: "CDN", "DNS TTL".
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the cache TTL." Does not address caching failures or retry amplification.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does a failed fetch return? Is the cache keyed per URL? Do retries use backoff and jitter? Are there clients per pod (how many)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Purge the cache and stop caching empty/failed values.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) failures are cached because retry swallows errors; (b) retries amplify load (3 attempts x pods); (c) no negative-cache distinction.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log cache puts with value size; compare upstream QPS to client QPS.
  5. Root cause: Wrong contract (error as a value) combined with decorator order that caches the degraded result.
  6. Fix: retries throw after exhaustion; cache only successes; backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker outside.
Fetcher f = new CircuitBreakerFetcher(new CachingFetcher(new RetryFetcher(new HttpFetcher(), 3)));
// RetryFetcher throws; CachingFetcher.computeIfAbsent does not store on exception
  1. Prevention: Tests that simulate upstream failure through the full stack; chaos tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Serving stale-on-error is useful but must be explicit (stale-if-error with a limit). Cache outside retry avoids retrying cached hits, but only if failures never enter the cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retry outside the cache? -> Each retry may hit the cache first; fine for successes, useless for failures.
  • Thundering herd on expiry? -> Single-flight / request coalescing.
  • Kotlin delegation to build the stack? -> by next reduces boilerplate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "resilient" client cached empty product lists during a brief outage; storefront showed zero products for 10 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shortens TTL only.
  • Hire: stops caching failures, fixes retry contract.
  • Strong hire: ordering analysis, breaker, backoff with jitter, stale-if-error design.

questions.promptHtml: Name five code smells you look for in a review, and the refactoring that cures each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows if you can turn gut feelings into specific, actionable review feedback.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Long method (extract method), God class (extract class, SRP), primitive obsession (value object like Money), switch on type (polymorphism or strategy), feature envy (move method). A smell is a hint to look, not proof of a bug.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Smell                 Sign                               Cure
Long parameter list   7+ params                          parameter object / builder
Shotgun surgery       one change touches 8 files         group by change reason
Divergent change      one class edited for many reasons  split (SRP)
Data clump            same 3 fields travel together      make a class
Message chain         a.b().c().d()                      hide delegate
Mutable global state  static mutable singleton           inject, immutable

Duplication is not always bad: two things that look alike but change independently should stay separate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: @JvmInline value class Money(val cents: Long)     // instead of Double price

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Naming smells without cures.
  • DRY-ing coincidental duplication.
  • Calling every long method a smell without checking readability.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is double for money a smell? -> Binary floats: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004; use integer minor units.
  2. Speculative generality? -> An interface with one implementation and no second in sight; delete.
  3. Which smells can tools catch? -> Complexity, length, duplication (Sonar, Detekt, Android Lint).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists smells. Senior ties each to a change-risk argument and a safe refactoring.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 2,000-line God class was edited by five teams, causing weekly merge conflicts and regressions.

questions.contextHtml:
A team wants to extract a pricing module from OrderService. The change is behaviour-preserving, but 213 of 480 unit tests fail. Each test has 6 to 9 mocks and verifies call order. Release is in 3 days.

verify(repo).findCart(id);
verify(pricing, times(1)).quote(any());
verify(tax).apply(any());
InOrder inOrder = inOrder(repo, pricing, tax);
inOrder.verify(repo).save(captor.capture());

CI shows 31 minutes total; the suite also takes 11 minutes of Spring context startup.
questions.promptHtml: How do you proceed so the refactoring is safe and the suite survives the next one?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Update all 213 tests." Repeats the cost every refactor and verifies nothing about behaviour.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tests protect real behaviour (price correctness, idempotent charges)? Is there an integration suite? Are repos hand-mocked everywhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a few characterization tests at the public boundary of OrderService using a fake repo; keep only high-value mocks.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) tests assert interactions rather than outcomes; (b) fakes are missing; (c) mocks of third-party/value types.
  4. How I'd verify each: Sample 10 failing tests: which asserts are about outcomes vs calls.
  5. Root cause: Tests are coupled to structure, so structure-only changes fail them.
  6. Fix: introduce InMemoryOrderRepo and assert on outcome.
var repo = new InMemoryOrderRepo();
var svc = new OrderService(repo, new Pricing(), FixedTax.of(18));
svc.place(cartOf(500));
assertEquals(Status.PAID, repo.find(id).status());
verify(gateway, times(1)).charge(any(), eq(590));   // only the side effect

Migrate by deleting a test only after a boundary test covers its behaviour; refactor in small commits. 7. Prevention: Guideline: mock only outgoing side effects and types you own; contract tests for fakes; cap mocks per test in review. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not delete tests to get green; do not attempt the extraction and the test rewrite in one commit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fake drift? -> Run one contract suite against fake and real (Testcontainers).
  • Slow context? -> Use plain constructors in unit tests; keep Spring for a few slices.
  • Time to do? -> Boundary tests first (1 day), extraction (1 day), tests migrate gradually.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments suite of 700 interaction-verifying tests was replaced by 80 outcome tests and a fake ledger; later refactors passed without edits.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: mass-edits tests.
  • Hire: characterization tests plus fakes.
  • Strong hire: staged plan, contract tests, rule for future mocks.

questions.contextHtml:
An Android app's crash-free rate dropped from 99.7% to 98.9% after a DI cleanup. LeakCanary shows CheckoutActivity retained after back navigation; native memory grows 40 MB per checkout; OOM crashes on 2 GB devices.

@Singleton
class AnalyticsTracker @Inject constructor(private val activity: Activity) { ... }
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object Providers {
    @Provides fun provideActivity(): Activity = currentActivity!!   // static holder
}
LeakCanary: GC ROOT static Providers.currentActivity
  -> CheckoutActivity (destroyed, still referenced)

Red herrings: "images in the cart", "RecyclerView".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the leak in DI terms and fix it without losing the feature.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set currentActivity = null in onDestroy." Fragile; the singleton still holds a stale instance.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why does the tracker need the Activity (screen name? context for resources)? Which components hold it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pass applicationContext instead of the Activity; hotfix release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a long-lived scope (Singleton) holds a short-lived object; (b) static holder; (c) listener not unregistered.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary trace, heap dump, Hilt component graph.
  5. Root cause: Scope mismatch: object lifetimes in the graph must be shorter-or-equal in dependents. A singleton must not depend on an Activity-scoped thing.
  6. Fix: inject @ApplicationContext; pass screen name as a method argument.
@Singleton
class AnalyticsTracker @Inject constructor(@ApplicationContext private val ctx: Context) {
    fun track(screen: String, event: String) { /* ... */ }
}
  1. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug builds; Hilt scope checks by design; code review rule: never hold Activity/View in singletons.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not use WeakReference as a bandage; do not use global mutable state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• @ActivityScoped alternative? -> Fine if the tracker should die with the screen.
  • Compile-time vs runtime DI? -> Dagger catches wrong scope wiring at build; Koin would crash at runtime.
  • ViewModel injection? -> Never inject Activity into it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "convenience" singleton holding the main Activity leaked 25 MB per navigation; moving to application context removed the OOM class entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: nulls the static field.
  • Hire: scope mismatch and application context.
  • Strong hire: lint/tests, alternatives, and build-time guarantees.

questions.promptHtml: How do you refactor a 400-line method with no tests in production code that cannot be down for a day?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests discipline: safety nets, small steps, and risk control.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: First add characterization tests that record current behaviour, then change in tiny steps (extract, rename, move), running tests and committing after each. Never mix refactoring with new behaviour. For big replacements use the strangler pattern behind a flag.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
characterization test -> small change -> run tests -> commit -> repeat
  • Characterization tests: feed real inputs, snapshot outputs, even weird ones.
  • Use IDE automated refactorings (rename, extract) because they are mechanically safe.
  • Seams: introduce interfaces at boundaries to isolate time, I/O.
  • Strangler fig: route a slice of traffic to the new module via a flag, compare results (shadow mode), then expand.
  • Rewrites from scratch fall into the second-system effect.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
double total(Order o) {
    Money subtotal = o.subtotal();
    return discounts.stream().reduce(subtotal, (m, d) -> d.apply(o, m), (a, b) -> b).value();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Refactoring without tests.
  • Mixing bug fixes into refactoring commits.
  • Big-bang rewrites.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test a method that hits the DB and clock? -> Extract seams and inject fakes.
  2. When don't you refactor? -> Code you will never touch again.
  3. How do you measure safety? -> Mutation testing, shadow-traffic comparison.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "write tests first". Senior: characterization, seams, strangler with shadow comparison, and cadence in small deployable commits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 3-week branch rewrite of a checkout flow was abandoned; the incremental approach shipped value weekly.

questions.contextHtml:
Invoices use double price throughout 140 files. Finance finds a daily 1-3 paise (cent-level) drift in totals; for 20k invoices a day reconciliation is off by up to Rs 140. Multi-currency support is next quarter.

subtotal = 0.1 + 0.2        -> 0.30000000000000004
Math.round(price * 100)/100 -> rounding done differently in 6 places
DB column: DECIMAL(10,2) in one table, FLOAT in two

Red herring: "just round at the end".
questions.promptHtml: Plan a migration to a safe money model while production keeps running.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Big-bang replacement of double with BigDecimal everywhere in one release.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Currencies and minor units? Rounding rules per jurisdiction? Which services consume the API? Can we do dual-writes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Centralize rounding into one function and add a reconciliation job to alert on drift.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) binary float accumulation; (b) inconsistent rounding modes; (c) FLOAT columns losing precision.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recompute a day's invoices with BigDecimal; diff per line; check column types.
  5. Root cause: Primitive obsession: a domain concept (money) is a raw double with no invariants.
  6. Fix: introduce Money value type and migrate edge-first.
public record Money(long minor, Currency currency) {
    public Money plus(Money o) { requireSame(o); return new Money(Math.addExact(minor, o.minor), currency); }
}

Steps: add Money and adapters at boundaries; migrate core calculation first; DB migrates DECIMAL/integer minor units via expand-contract; dual-run old and new and compare; remove double APIs last. 7. Prevention: Lint rule banning double in domain packages; property-based tests (associativity); reconciliation alerts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: BigDecimal is slower and verbose but fine for invoices; avoid float; do not convert at the end only.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Splitting Rs 100 among 3? -> Allocation with remainder distribution.
  • API compatibility? -> Keep the JSON field as string/minor units with a version.
  • Kotlin? -> @JvmInline value class gives type safety with low overhead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A billing system with 6 rounding spots was unified into one Money type; the monthly mismatch dropped to zero and audit time shrank.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "round at the end".
  • Hire: Money type with minor units and staged migration.
  • Strong hire: shadow comparison, DB expand-contract, allocation edge cases.

questions.contextHtml:
A team made ReadOnlyCart extends Cart to reuse display code, throwing from mutators. The checkout page crashes for 0.4% of users (those on the shared-link view) with UnsupportedOperationException, and a pricing job silently skips carts.

class Cart {
    public void add(Item i) { items.add(i); }
    public double total() { /* sums items */ }
    public void applyCoupon(Coupon c) { discounts.add(c); }
}
class ReadOnlyCart extends Cart {
    @Override public void add(Item i) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    @Override public void applyCoupon(Coupon c) { /* ignored */ }
}
void checkout(Cart c) { c.applyCoupon(promo); c.add(freeGift); pay(c.total()); }

Red herring: "caller should catch the exception".
questions.promptHtml: What principle is violated, and how do you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Callers must check instanceof ReadOnlyCart." Spreads the type check everywhere.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which operations does the display code need? Are there other read-only views? Who creates ReadOnlyCart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make shared-link view not reach checkout; add guard at the boundary.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) LSP violation: subtype strengthens preconditions/weakens postconditions; (b) one fat type serving two roles; (c) ignored applyCoupon is a silent behavioural change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Contract tests applied to Cart and all subclasses; code search for instanceof.
  5. Root cause: Inheriting to reuse code created a subtype that cannot honour the base contract.
  6. Fix: split interfaces, compose.
interface CartView { List<Item> items(); Money total(); }
interface EditableCart extends CartView { void add(Item i); void applyCoupon(Coupon c); }
final class ReadOnlyCartView implements CartView {      // composition: wraps a snapshot
    private final List<Item> items; /* copy in */ 
}
void checkout(EditableCart c) { ... }       // types prevent the bug
  1. Prevention: LSP contract test suite; "no throwing UnsupportedOperationException in overrides" review rule; interface segregation.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Two interfaces add types; but they move a runtime failure to compile time. I would not keep a boolean readOnly flag in a single class.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• JDK precedent? -> Collections.unmodifiableList violates List's mutators; known compromise.
  • Kotlin approach? -> Read-only List vs MutableList interfaces.
  • Square extends Rectangle? -> Same: setting width changes height, breaking caller assumptions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "frozen" subclass of a domain entity threw in 3% of batch jobs; splitting read and write interfaces turned all of them into compile errors fixed in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: handles exceptions at callers.
  • Hire: names LSP, redesigns with interfaces.
  • Strong hire: contract tests, ISP, compile-time enforcement and JDK analogies.
